subsection: 2. Costs and revenue streams: fixed, variable and recurring income

notes.h: Costs, revenue and profit: the starting point
notes.b: A cost is money a business spends to operate, and revenue is money it earns from sales and other sources. Everything else in this topic is about how those two behave.
points: Profit equals total revenue minus total costs, so a business makes a profit when revenue is bigger than costs. A loss is the reverse, when costs are bigger than revenue.
Revenue is not the same as profit. Revenue is the income coming in, while profit is what is left after the costs are taken away, so a business with high revenue can still make a loss.
The business model canvas (a tool that maps out a business model) shows both sides: its cost structure block lists the costs and its revenue streams block lists the income sources.
notes.tip: Common mistake: treating revenue and profit as the same thing. Write revenue as income and profit as revenue minus costs.

notes.b: Costs are classified by how they behave as output (the number of units made or served) changes. Each cost belongs to one group, so learn the test for each.
points: Fixed costs stay the same in total whatever the level of output in the short run, such as rent, insurance and the salaries of permanent staff. A sample café pays the same rent whether it serves ten customers or a thousand.
Variable costs change directly with output, such as raw materials, packaging and wages paid per item made. Make more units and the total rises; make none and it falls to zero.
The classification test is to ask: does the total change if output doubles? If it does, the cost is variable. If it stays the same, it is fixed.
Wages depend on how they are paid. A permanent salary is fixed, but wages linked to output, such as pay per item made, are variable.
Fixed costs are sometimes called indirect costs and variable costs direct costs, because variable costs can be traced straight to each unit made.
Total cost equals fixed costs plus variable costs at a given level of output, so total cost rises with output only because the variable part rises.
notes.tip: A question that lists costs wants each cost named, its type (fixed or variable) and a link to the business. Common mistake: classing insurance or permanent salaries as variable. Insurance does not change with output, so a list of variable costs that includes it is wrong.

notes.b: Some costs do not fit neatly into either group because they have a fixed part and a part that moves with use.
points: A semi-variable cost has a fixed element and a usage element. Electricity is the standard example: a standing charge is paid whatever happens, plus a usage charge that rises with the units used.
When a question offers only fixed or variable, classify the item by its main behaviour. Apply the doubling test to the biggest part of the bill and say which element you are treating as the main one.

Do not give a flat verdict that electricity is fixed or that it is variable. Explain that it has both elements, then classify it by the one that dominates in the business in the question, because a factory running machines all day uses far more than a small office.
notes.tip: Show the reasoning, not just the label: name the fixed element, name the usage element, then state which dominates.

notes.b: Costs can also be grouped by when they arise in the life of the business. This is a different grouping from fixed and variable, and it answers a different question.
points: Start-up costs are incurred before trading begins, such as legal fees, fit-out of premises, equipment and initial stock.
Running costs are the ongoing costs of operating once trading starts, such as wages, rent, utilities and marketing.
Start-up costs are usually one-off, so they weigh heavily on cash in the early months, when the business has paid out money but has not yet earned any.
A business that underestimates its running costs can run short of cash even when sales are growing, because the money going out each month can still be more than the money coming in.
One cost can be described both ways. Rent is a running cost, because it is paid every month once trading starts, and it is also a fixed cost, because it does not change with output.
notes.tip: Fixed and variable describe behaviour as output changes. Start-up and running describe timing. If a question asks for one, do not answer with the other.

notes.b: A revenue stream is a source of income. The main difference between streams is how often the customer pays, and a business can combine several at once.
points: A one-off transaction is a single sale where the customer pays once, such as buying a laptop or a meal in a restaurant. Income only continues if the business finds a new sale each time.
Recurring revenue is repeated income. It makes cash flow easier to predict, because the business can estimate next month's income before the month begins.
A subscription is a regular fee for continued access to a product or service, such as a monthly gym membership.

Licensing earns fees for letting others use intellectual property (creations of the mind that the owner has legal rights over) such as a brand, patent or software. A licence fee can be one-off or recurring, so classify it from the example given.
Usage fees charge customers according to how much they use a service, such as a per-unit charge for mobile data, so the more the customer uses, the more the business earns.
Advertising revenue comes from selling space or airtime to other businesses, which is how many free apps and websites earn their income even though users pay nothing.
A business can combine streams. A sample software firm might sell a one-off set-up service, a monthly subscription and advertising space in its app.
notes.tip: Common mistake: treating a one-off sale as a subscription. Identify the stream, then say why recurring income helps: predictable cash.

notes.b: Break-even is the output at which total revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero. To find it you need to know how much each unit sold contributes towards the fixed costs.
points: Profit equals total revenue minus total costs. Above break-even there is a profit and below it there is a loss.
Contribution per unit is the selling price minus the variable cost per unit. It is the amount each sale has left over after its own variable costs, and it goes towards covering fixed costs.
Break-even quantity equals fixed costs divided by contribution per unit, because that is how many units are needed to cover the fixed costs.
Sample figures: fixed costs of €6,000, a selling price of €15 and a variable cost of €9 give a contribution of €6 and a break-even of 1,000 units, since 6,000 divided by 6 is 1,000.
Above break-even each extra unit adds to profit, while below it the business makes a loss.
notes.tip: If a calculation is set, show the formula, the substitution and the unit. Common mistake: dividing by the selling price instead of by the contribution per unit.

notes.h: Why costs and revenue change through the life cycle
notes.b: The product life cycle has four stages: introduction, growth, maturity and decline. The business life cycle is the business's own path from start-up through growth to maturity, and possibly decline or renewal. Costs and revenue change at each stage for a reason.
points: Introduction: sales are low and promotion costs are high, because customers must be told the product exists. The business may make a loss.
Growth: sales rise quickly and unit costs fall as output increases, because fixed costs are spread over more units. Profit grows.
Maturity: sales level off and competition increases. Price pressure, such as discounting to keep customers, reduces margins.
Decline: sales fall, so the business may cut costs, narrow its range or withdraw the product, because it cannot keep paying for a product that no longer sells enough.
Over the business life cycle the mix of costs and revenue streams shifts too. A mature firm may rely more on recurring income, because it has built up a loyal customer base.
notes.tip: To explain a change, give the stage, the change, the reason and the effect on profit. Common mistake: naming the stages without saying what happens to costs or revenue.

notes.b: The way a business chooses its costs and charges its customers raises ethical, sustainability and digital questions that exam answers can apply.
points: Ethical charging means fair and clear prices. Subscription terms should be easy to understand and easy to cancel, and fees should not be hidden from customers.
Paying workers fairly is a cost an ethical business accepts even when cheaper options exist.
Sustainable materials, energy-efficient equipment and waste reduction change costs. They usually raise start-up costs but lower running costs over time, for example through smaller energy bills.

Reuse, repair and take-back schemes can become new revenue streams in a circular economy: a model of production and consumption which extends the life cycle of products, reduces waste, and creates further value.
Software-as-a-service subscriptions and cloud services charged by usage change variable cost, because the bill follows how much the business uses.
In-app advertising, platform fees and usage-based pricing are digital revenue streams, which means income can scale with use.

notes.h: Evaluation: how the mix affects risk
notes.b: The mix of costs and revenue streams affects a business's risk as well as its profit.
points: A business dependent on one-off sales has less predictable cash flow than one with recurring income, because it cannot be sure of next month's sales.
High fixed costs make profit sensitive to changes in sales, so a small fall in sales can turn a profit into a loss. The fixed costs must still be paid.
Moving to subscriptions can build customer loyalty, but customers may cancel if the service stops providing value.

questions.prompt: A café owner is opening a coffee shop in Galway. Classify the main costs as fixed, variable or semi-variable, distinguish start-up costs from running costs, and explain how costs and revenue would change as the shop moves through the business life cycle.
questions.model: Classification: rent, insurance and permanent staff salaries are fixed; coffee beans, milk, cups and packaging are variable; electricity is semi-variable. Start-up: the espresso machine, fit-out, licences, legal fees and initial stock, all paid before the first sale. Running: rent, utilities, staff wages and marketing that continue once trading starts. Revenue: mainly one-off sales of coffee, which could be supplemented by recurring income from a loyalty subscription or regular sales of bags of beans. Life cycle: in the introduction stage marketing spend is high and sales low, so a loss is likely; in the growth stage sales rise and unit costs fall; in the maturity stage competition squeezes prices, so the owner must control costs closely.

questions.prompt: A business has fixed costs of €10,000, a selling price of €20 per unit and a variable cost of €12 per unit. Calculate its break-even quantity and explain what happens to profit above that level of output.
questions.model: Contribution per unit is €20 minus €12, which is €8. Break-even quantity is €10,000 divided by €8, which is 1,250 units. Above 1,250 units each additional unit adds €8 to profit, because the contribution covers the unit's own variable cost and the fixed costs have already been covered.
